title: Woman shot dead by Calgary police on Christmas 'was like a Disney princess,' say friends
article: "She was like a Disney princess."
Those are the words a friend uses to describe Stacey Perry - a 29-year-old mother who was shot and killed by Calgary police on Christmas morning.
"(She was) soft-spoken, wore dresses all the time, loved life (and) was so vibrant and full of life," said Perry's friend, Carolyn Rennie, holding back emotions.
"Every time I talked to her, she had such a big heart," Rennie said in a Friday interview with Postmedia. "She cared so much for everyone else."
Rennie met Perry last June at an addiction treatment centre in Salmon Arm, B.C - a city in which Perry would eventually live.
"(When I met her) she was going through a lot of challenges and we were going to support groups together," said Rennie.

"Then, after her stay, she decided she would move here," recalled Rennie. "She got a place here. Her (nine-year-old) daughter was back in Edmonton, so she would visit her when she could. I hooked her (Perry) up with a job at an insurance company here and things were good for four or five months."

The shooting of Perry is being investigated by the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT). After a wild driving spree in Calgary, sources say Perry's car pinned a female officer to another vehicle before a 10-year veteran of the Calgary Police Service fired his gun, killing Perry.
Vincent Church, an ex-boyfriend who remained close with Perry, called her a vibrant and caring young woman who dealt with alcohol and substance addictions.
"She was a well-meaning person (who was) battling some addictions and would often call and look for guidance or advice," said Church, who met Perry four years ago in Fort McMurray.
"Stacey always had a good heart. It was hard for her, but she was doing her best ... She was trying very hard to get through all of that."
Church said after Perry left the rehabilitation facility, she was continuing academic studies in medical office administration.
Perry was a woman who would panic when addiction got the best of her, Church said, adding he believes that's what may have caused Perry's flight from police, leading to her eventual death.
"That panic could take several forms; it would cause her to run away from a situation," said Church. "It wouldn't happen often, but that panic would set in."

"(The day she was shot) she may have undoubtedly had a bad time, or bad episode or somebody threatened her or did something to her to cause her to panic," he said. "It would probably give her the fight or flight reflexes and when she became distressed, she didn't always make the best decisions."

Just after midnight on Christmas morning, Perry was driving erratically near 9th Avenue and Blackfoot Trail S.E. in a grey Honda sedan with a B.C. licence plate. Officers tried to stop her vehicle on suspicion of impaired driving.
However, she failed to pull over. Driving through the city's northwest, police said she was running red lights at fluctuating speeds.
Two more traffic stops were attempted, also unsuccessfully, around 12:30 a.m. Police stopped following the vehicle about 10 minutes later, citing "safety reasons."

Less than two hours later, police received a call about a driver "running red lights and doing U-turns" in the northeast community of Falconridge. Officers located the same grey Honda sedan from earlier, being driven the wrong way into oncoming lanes of traffic throughout northeast Calgary.

Police attempted a controlled stop of the sedan, which was entering onto McKnight Boulevard from Stoney Trail, by positioning a police vehicle in the front of the sedan and additional police vehicles on each side of, and behind, the car.
As officers began to exit their vehicles, "the sedan was put in motion," according to ASIRT, in a statement issued Thursday.
Rennie said she didn't know what happened to Perry the morning she was killed.
"What I know is that whatever happened that night would've been completely out of fear and completely not something that she would ever do in a sober, sane and safe mind," Rennie said.

"She's not this terrible person running through the streets. People think of people who have addiction problems like awful people and we are just normal people who have bad things happen to us," she said.
"I hope for anyone struggling, they talk and admit what is going on. That's the only way we can get help."
On Thursday, Les Kaminski, president of the Calgary Police Association, called the incident a tragic circumstance.
"We are very, very fortunate - extremely fortunate - that we don't have a police officer that was injured or even killed during that incident," he said.

"It was a high-risk ... very emotional, high-crisis incident and it's very fortunate we don't have a police officer dead. In my 33 years, (this was) the first time we have ever had a critical incident like this on Christmas Day - it was heart-wrenching on a number of levels."
